def-log-convention.title: The logarithm convention
body: The notation $\log$ means $\log_2$, except where changing the base changes only an absolute constant. In particular, the logarithms in $T$ in Proposition 3.2, $r$ and $\ell$ in equation (6), and $L$ in equation (5) are exactly base two.

The notation log means log₂, except where changing the base changes only an absolute constant. In particular, the logarithms in T in Proposition 3.2, r and ℓ in equation (6), and L in equation (5) are exactly base two.

def-partial-query.title: Partial Boolean functions and their promises
body: A partial Boolean function is a pair $(D,P)$ with $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^N$ and $P:D\to\{0,1\}$. An algorithm computes it if it is correct, with the stated error, on every $x\in D$; its behaviour outside $D$ is unconstrained.

A partial Boolean function is a pair (D, P) with D ⊆ the set of N-bit strings and P: D → bits. An algorithm computes it if it is correct, with the stated error, on every x ∈ D; its behaviour outside D is unconstrained.

title: Randomized query complexity $R(f)$
Randomized query complexity R(f)
body: For a possibly partial Boolean function $f$, $R(f)$ is the least $q$ for which a probability distribution on deterministic decision trees of depth at most $q$ satisfies $\Pr[T(x)=f(x)]\ge 2/3$ for every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The query cap holds on every branch and for every coin outcome.

For a possibly partial Boolean function f, R(f) is the least q for which a probability distribution on deterministic decision trees of depth at most q satisfies Pr[T(x) = f(x)] ≥ 2/3 for every x ∈ dom f. The query cap holds on every branch and for every coin outcome.

def-query-oracle.title: The bit-query oracle
body: For $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the bit oracle is the self-inverse unitary $O_x\lvert i,b,z\rangle=\lvert i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle$, where $i\in[n]$, $b$ is a bit, and $z$ is a workspace label.
For x ∈ the set of n-bit strings, the bit oracle is the self-inverse unitary Oₓ|i, b, z⟩ = |i, b ⊕ xᵢ, z⟩, where i ∈ [n], b is a bit, and z is a workspace label.

title: Quantum query complexity $Q(f)$
Quantum query complexity Q(f)
body: $Q(f)$ is the least $q$ for which a quantum algorithm, with unrestricted query-free computation between uses of $O_x$ and at most $q$ queries on every branch, including every measurement outcome, outputs $f(x)$ with probability at least $2/3$ for every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$.

Q(f) is the least q for which a quantum algorithm, with unrestricted query-free computation between uses of Oₓ and at most q queries on every branch, including every measurement outcome, outputs f(x) with probability at least 2/3 for every x ∈ dom f.

title: Defining the optimal exponent $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}$
Defining the optimal exponent αₜₒₜ
body: The exponent $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the infimum of all $\alpha\ge0$ for which there exists a finite constant $C_\alpha$ such that, for every $n\ge1$ and every total function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$, $R(f)\le C_\alpha(1+Q(f))^\alpha$.
The exponent αₜₒₜ is the infimum of all α ≥ 0 for which there exists a finite constant Cα such that, for every n ≥ 1 and every total function f: n-bit strings → bits, R(f) ≤ Cα(1 + Q(f))ᵅ.

eq-2.title: The separating family’s query bounds
body: For each fixed integer $k\ge2$ and all sufficiently large powers of four $m$, $Q(F_{k,m})\le C_k\sqrt m(\log m)^{b_k}$ and $R(F_{k,m})\ge c_km^{2-1/k}/(\log m)^2$, where $c_k,C_k,b_k>0$ depend only on $k$.
For each fixed integer k ≥ 2 and all sufficiently large powers of four m, Q(Fₖ,ₘ) ≤ Cₖ√m(log m)^(bₖ) and R(Fₖ,ₘ) ≥ cₖm^(2 − 1/k)/(log m)², where cₖ, Cₖ, bₖ > 0 depend only on k.

title: The optimal universal exponent is $4$
The optimal universal exponent is 4
body: $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}=4$. More precisely, $R(f)=O((1+Q(f))^4)$ for every total Boolean function $f$, and the two bounds in equation (2) hold for each fixed integer $k\ge2$.
αₜₒₜ = 4. More precisely, R(f) = O((1 + Q(f))⁴) for every total Boolean function f, and the two bounds in equation (2) hold for each fixed integer k ≥ 2.

cor-cubic-refuted.title: Refuting the universal cubic conjecture
body: The assertion $R(f)=O(Q(f)^3)$ for all total Boolean functions $f$ is false, refuting Conjecture 2 of reference [3]: no constant $C$ satisfies $R(f)\le C Q(f)^3$ for every total $f$.
The assertion R(f) = O(Q(f)³) for all total Boolean functions f is false, refuting Conjecture 2 of reference [3]: no constant C satisfies R(f) ≤ C Q(f)³ for every total f.

def-walsh-sign.title: Walsh matrices, uniform states, and sign diagonals
body: Let $m=4^t$. The normalized Walsh–Hadamard matrix $H$ has dimensions $m\times m$ and entries $H_{a,b}=m^{-1/2}(-1)^{\langle a,b\rangle}$ for $a,b\in\{0,1\}^{\log_2 m}$. Set $u=m^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}$. Identify a bit $a$ with the sign $(-1)^a$. For $z\in\{\pm1\}^m$, set $D_z=\operatorname{diag}(z)$.

Let m = 4ᵗ. The normalized Walsh–Hadamard matrix H has dimensions m × m and entries Hₐ,ᵦ = m⁻¹ᐟ²(−1)^⟨a,b⟩ for a, b ∈ the set of binary strings of length log₂ m. Set u = m⁻¹ᐟ²(1, …, 1)ᵀ. Identify a bit a with the sign (−1)ᵃ. For z ∈ the set of length-m sign vectors, set D(z) = diag(z).

eq-3.title: The Forrelation statistic and promise threshold
body: For $z_1,\ldots,z_k\in\{\pm1\}^m$, define $\Phi(z_1,\ldots,z_k)=u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_1}HD_{z_2}H\cdots HD_{z_k}u$, with $k$ diagonal matrices and $k-1$ copies of $H$, and set $\delta=2^{-5k}$.
For z₁, …, zₖ ∈ the set of length-m sign vectors, define Φ(z₁, …, zₖ) = uᵀD(z₁)HD(z₂)H⋯HD(zₖ)u, with k diagonal matrices and k − 1 copies of H, and set δ = 2^(−5k).

eq-4.title: The partial Forrelation function
body: The partial function $P=P_{k,m}$ on $km$ bits is $1$ when $\Phi\ge\delta$, $0$ when $|\Phi|\le\delta/2$, and undefined otherwise. These two cases are disjoint.
The partial function P = Pₖ,ₘ on km bits is 1 when Φ ≥ δ, 0 when |Φ| ≤ δ/2, and undefined otherwise. These two cases are disjoint.

eq-5.title: The randomized lower-bound threshold
body: Define $L=L_{k,m}=\left\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/(\log_2m)^2\right\rfloor$.
Define L = Lₖ,ₘ = ⌊m^(1 − 1/k)/(log₂ m)²⌋.

claim-bs-to-L.title: The Bansal–Sinha bound exceeds the chosen threshold
body: For each fixed $k\ge2$ and the positive constant $c$ in the Bansal–Sinha bound, all sufficiently large powers of four $m$ satisfy $ck^{-29}\bigl(m/\log(km)\bigr)^{1-1/k}>\left\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/(\log_2m)^2\right\rfloor$.
For each fixed k ≥ 2 and the positive constant c in the Bansal–Sinha bound, all sufficiently large powers of four m satisfy ck⁻²⁹(m/log(km))^(1 − 1/k) > ⌊m^(1 − 1/k)/(log₂ m)²⌋.

lem-2.1.i.title: The randomized lower bound for Forrelation
body: For each fixed $k\ge2$ and all sufficiently large powers of four $m$, $R(P_{k,m})>L$, where $L$ is defined in equation (5).
For each fixed k ≥ 2 and all sufficiently large powers of four m, R(Pₖ,ₘ) > L, where L is defined in equation (5).

title: The projection succeeds with probability $\Phi^2$
The projection succeeds with probability Φ²
body: Prepare $u$, apply $D_{z_1}H\cdots HD_{z_k}$ from right to left, and measure the projection onto $u$. Each sign diagonal uses one bit query through phase kickback; $H$ and the projection use no queries. The success probability is exactly $\Phi^2$, at least $\delta^2$ on inputs with value one and at most $\delta^2/4$ on inputs with value zero.

Prepare u, apply D(z₁)H⋯HD(zₖ) from right to left, and measure the projection onto u. Each sign diagonal uses one bit query through phase kickback; H and the projection use no queries. The success probability is exactly Φ², at least δ² on inputs with value one and at most δ²/4 on inputs with value zero.

lem-2.1.ii.title: An accurate coherent Forrelation algorithm
body: For every $0<\eta<1/2$, there is a quantum algorithm using $O_k(1+\log(1/\eta))$ bit queries that outputs $P_{k,m}(z)$ with error at most $\eta$ for every $z\in\operatorname{dom}P$. It has a coherent implementation retaining all workspace. On every input, promised or not, measuring its output register yields a bit.

For every 0 < η < 1/2, there is a quantum algorithm using Oₖ(1 + log(1/η)) bit queries that outputs Pₖ,ₘ(z) with error at most η for every z ∈ dom P. It has a coherent implementation retaining all workspace. On every input, promised or not, measuring its output register yields a bit.

claim-N-phi.title: The integer numerator and normalization
body: With $W=\sqrt m\,H$ having entries $\pm1$, the quantity $N=z_1^{\mathsf T}WD_{z_2}W\cdots WD_{z_k}(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}$ is an integer, $\Phi=N/M_{k,m}$, and $M_{k,m}=m(\sqrt m)^{k-1}$ is a positive integer because $m$ is a power of four.
With W = √m H having entries ±1, the quantity N = z₁ᵀWD(z₂)W⋯WD(zₖ)(1, …, 1)ᵀ is an integer, Φ = N/Mₖ,ₘ, and Mₖ,ₘ = m(√m)^(k − 1) is a positive integer because m is a power of four.

claim-integer-tests.title: The exact integer promise tests
body: The comparison $\Phi\ge\delta$ is equivalent to $2^{5k}N\ge M_{k,m}$, and $|\Phi|\le\delta/2$ is equivalent to $2^{5k+1}|N|\le M_{k,m}$. The bit $d$ is the disjunction of these comparisons, and $b$ is the first comparison.
The comparison Φ ≥ δ is equivalent to 2^(5k)N ≥ Mₖ,ₘ, and |Φ| ≤ δ/2 is equivalent to 2^(5k + 1)|N| ≤ Mₖ,ₘ. The bit d is the disjunction of these comparisons, and b is the first comparison.

claim-circuit-size.title: Computing the numerator with a small Boolean circuit
body: Compute $N$ using $k-1$ unnormalized Walsh–Hadamard transforms, coordinate sign changes, and a final signed sum. Each transform uses $O(m\log m)$ additions and subtractions. All intermediate integers have absolute value at most $m^{O(k)}$, so $O_k(\log m)$ bits suffice. The resulting Boolean circuit has size $O_k(m(\log m)^2)$.

Compute N using k − 1 unnormalized Walsh–Hadamard transforms, coordinate sign changes, and a final signed sum. Each transform uses O(m log m) additions and subtractions. All intermediate integers have absolute value at most m^O(k), so Oₖ(log m) bits suffice. The resulting Boolean circuit has size Oₖ(m(log m)²).

lem-2.1.iii.title: An exact circuit for the promise and value
body: There is a Boolean circuit $C=C_{k,m}$ with fan-in at most two and size $S=S_{k,m}=O_k(m(\log m)^2)$, counting non-input gates, whose output bits $d,b$ satisfy, for every input $z$, $d=1$ if and only if $P_{k,m}$ is defined at $z$, and $d=1$ implies $b=P_{k,m}(z)$. The circuit computes these outputs exactly on every input.

There is a Boolean circuit C = Cₖ,ₘ with fan-in at most two and size S = Sₖ,ₘ = Oₖ(m(log m)²), counting non-input gates, whose output bits d, b satisfy, for every input z, d = 1 if and only if Pₖ,ₘ is defined at z, and d = 1 implies b = Pₖ,ₘ(z). The circuit computes these outputs exactly on every input.

lem-2.1.title: The three Forrelation ingredients
body: For each fixed $k\ge2$, the conclusions of all three parts of Lemma 2.1 hold together: the randomized lower bound in part (i), the coherent quantum algorithm in part (ii), and the exact Boolean circuit in part (iii).

For each fixed k ≥ 2, the conclusions of all three parts of Lemma 2.1 hold together: the randomized lower bound in part (i), the coherent quantum algorithm in part (ii), and the exact Boolean circuit in part (iii).

def-transcript.title: Circuit transcripts
def-transcript.body: For a fixed circuit, a transcript assigns a proposed bit to each non-input gate, including output gates. Input-wire values are read from the actual input rather than copied into the transcript.

eq-6.title: The address and pointer lengths
body: Set $r=\lceil20\log_2m\rceil$ and $\ell=\log_2m$.
Set r = ⌈20 log₂ m⌉ and ℓ = log₂ m.

def-column-layout.title: The input’s columns, cells, and certificates
body: The input has $m$ columns. Column $i$ contains a string $X_i\in\{0,1\}^m$, strings $A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}\in\{0,1\}^{km}$ with no promise, and a cell $B_{i,s}$ for each $s\in\{0,1\}^r$. Each cell holds, for every $j\ne i$, a pointer $p_{i,s,j}\in[m]$ encoded in $\ell$ bits by a fixed bijection, and, for every $h\in[r]$, an alleged evaluation transcript of $C_{k,m}$ on $A_{i,h}$.

The input has m columns. Column i contains a string Xᵢ ∈ the set of m-bit strings, strings Aᵢ,₁, …, Aᵢ,ᵣ ∈ the set of km-bit strings with no promise, and a cell Bᵢ,ₛ for each s ∈ the set of r-bit strings. Each cell holds, for every j ≠ i, a pointer pᵢ,ₛ,ⱼ ∈ [m] encoded in ℓ bits by a fixed bijection, and, for every h ∈ [r], an alleged evaluation transcript of Cₖ,ₘ on Aᵢ,ₕ.

def-eval-transcript.title: Correct evaluation transcripts
body: An evaluation transcript of $C_{k,m}$ on $A_{i,h}$ contains one bit for each non-input gate, including output gates; these gates are counted by $S$. The transcript is correct if and only if every bit equals the true value of its gate on input $A_{i,h}$.

An evaluation transcript of Cₖ,ₘ on Aᵢ,ₕ contains one bit for each non-input gate, including output gates; these gates are counted by S. The transcript is correct if and only if every bit equals the true value of its gate on input Aᵢ,ₕ.

eq-7.title: A column’s true address
body: If every $P(A_{i,h})$ is defined, the true address of column $i$ is $s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\ldots,P(A_{i,r}))\in\{0,1\}^r$.
If every P(Aᵢ,ₕ) is defined, the true address of column i is sᵢ = (P(Aᵢ,₁), …, P(Aᵢ,ᵣ)) ∈ the set of r-bit strings.

eq-8.title: Pointers to zeros in every other column
body: The outward pointer condition at address $s$ is $X_j[p_{i,s,j}]=0$ for every $j\ne i$. Equation (8) of the paper is the case $s=s_i$.
The outward pointer condition at address s is Xⱼ[pᵢ,ₛ,ⱼ] = 0 for every j ≠ i. Equation (8) of the paper is the case s = sᵢ.

def-winner.title: Winning columns
body: Column $i$ is a winner if and only if $X_i=1^m$, every $P(A_{i,h})$ is defined, and the cell $B_{i,s_i}$ contains correct evaluation transcripts on all $A_{i,h}$ and pointers satisfying equation (8).
Column i is a winner if and only if Xᵢ = 1ᵐ, every P(Aᵢ,ₕ) is defined, and the cell Bᵢ,ₛᵢ contains correct evaluation transcripts on all Aᵢ,ₕ and pointers satisfying equation (8).

def-F.title: The total function detects a winning column
body: The value $F_{k,m}(y)$ is $1$ if some column of $y$ is a winner, and $0$ otherwise. This defines a total Boolean function on all input bit strings.
The value Fₖ,ₘ(y) is 1 if some column of y is a winner, and 0 otherwise. This defines a total Boolean function on all input bit strings.

cor-unique-winner.title: Uniqueness of the winning column
cor-unique-winner.body: For every input, at most one column is a winner.

def-win-at-address.title: Winning at a specified address
body: $\operatorname{WinsAt}(y,i,s)$ holds if and only if $X_i=1^m$, for every $h$ the transcript in $B_{i,s}$ on $A_{i,h}$ is correct with outputs $d=1$ and $b=s_h$, and equation (8) holds at $s$. The paper’s wording, “$i$ is a winner and $s=s_i$,” is equivalent by the equivalence between the address test and the winner condition.

WinsAt(y, i, s) holds if and only if Xᵢ = 1ᵐ, for every h the transcript in Bᵢ,ₛ on Aᵢ,ₕ is correct with outputs d = 1 and b = sₕ, and equation (8) holds at s. The paper’s wording, “i is a winner and s = sᵢ,” is equivalent by the equivalence between the address test and the winner condition.

title: Counting the $K_{k,m}$ local winner tests
Counting the K(k, m) local winner tests
body: Kₖ,ₘ = m + (m − 1) + r(Sₖ,ₘ + 2) = Oₖ(m(log m)³).

lem-2.2.i.title: Local tests characterize winning at an address
body: For every input $y$ and $(i,s)\in[m]\times\{0,1\}^r$: $i$ wins at $s$ if and only if all $K_{k,m}$ tests pass, namely (a) $X_i[b]=1$ for each $b$; (b) for each $j\ne i$, $X_j[p_{i,s,j}]=0$; (c) for each $h$ and each non-input gate, the claimed value equals the gate function of its predecessors, read from the transcript or from $A_{i,h}$; (d) for each $h$, claimed $d=1$ and claimed $b=s_h$. Each test is computed by a deterministic adaptive bit-query decision tree of depth at most $\max(3,\ell+1)$, which is $\ell+1$ for $m\ge4$: a pointer test reads $\ell$ pointer bits, then the one target bit they select, while gate tests read at most three fixed bits. A pointer test is not a function of a small fixed set of bits: it can depend on all $\ell+m$ pointer and target coordinates.

For every input y and (i, s) ∈ [m] × the set of length-r binary strings: i wins at s if and only if all Kₖ,ₘ tests pass, namely (a) Xᵢ[b] = 1 for each b; (b) for each j ≠ i, Xⱼ[pᵢ,ₛ,ⱼ] = 0; (c) for each h and each non-input gate, the claimed value equals the gate function of its predecessors, read from the transcript or from Aᵢ,ₕ; (d) for each h, claimed d = 1 and claimed b = sₕ. Each test is computed by a deterministic adaptive bit-query decision tree of depth at most max(3, ℓ + 1), which is ℓ + 1 for m ≥ 4: a pointer test reads ℓ pointer bits, then the one target bit they select, while gate tests read at most three fixed bits. A pointer test is not a function of a small fixed set of bits: it can depend on all ℓ + m pointer and target coordinates.

lem-2.2.ii.title: Exact coherent evaluation of local tests
body: Each test is evaluated exactly with $O(\log m)$ bit queries, also coherently with the same bound with test indices in superposition. The number of tests and the indexing convention are the same for every $(i,s)$.

Each test is evaluated exactly with O(log m) bit queries, also coherently with the same bound with test indices in superposition. The number of tests and the indexing convention are the same for every (i, s).

lem-2.2.title: Local winner tests and their coherent evaluation
lem-2.2.body: Winning at a specified address is equivalent to passing every local test in Lemma 2.2(i). Each of these tests admits the exact coherent evaluation in Lemma 2.2(ii).

cor-local-dichotomy.title: Passing and failing addresses distinguish winners
cor-local-dichotomy.body: A winner has an address at which every test passes; a nonwinner has a failing test at every address.

def-grover-trial.title: Random Grover trials with bounded repetition
body: $M=\lceil10/\sqrt{\gamma}\rceil$. A trial picks with probability $1/2$ $\ell=0$, and with probability $1/2$ a uniform $\ell\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$, applies $\ell$ Grover iterations to $A\lvert0\rangle$, and measures the success bit. The procedure runs $\lceil\log(1/\eta)/\log(40/31)\rceil$ trials with fresh registers, stopping at the first success.

M = ⌈10/√γ⌉. A trial picks with probability 1/2 ℓ = 0, and with probability 1/2 a uniform ℓ in the integers from 0 through M − 1, applies ℓ Grover iterations to A|0⟩, and measures the success bit. The procedure runs ⌈log(1/η)/log(40/31)⌉ trials with fresh registers, stopping at the first success.

claim-grover-state.title: Grover rotation preserves the successful direction
body: For $0<p<1$ write $A\lvert0\rangle=\sin(\theta)\lvert g\rangle+\cos(\theta)\lvert b\rangle$, $0<\theta<\pi/2$, with $g,b$ normalized in the successful and unsuccessful subspaces. After $\ell$ Grover iterations the state is $\sin((2\ell+1)\theta)\lvert g\rangle+\cos((2\ell+1)\theta)\lvert b\rangle$. Hence measuring success yields $\lvert g\rangle$ up to global phase, independently of $\ell$.

For 0 < p < 1 write A|0⟩ = sin(θ)|g⟩ + cos(θ)|b⟩, 0 < θ < π/2, with g, b normalized in the successful and unsuccessful subspaces. After ℓ Grover iterations the state is sin((2ℓ + 1)θ)|g⟩ + cos((2ℓ + 1)θ)|b⟩. Hence measuring success yields |g⟩ up to global phase, independently of ℓ.

claim-sin2theta.title: The promised success probability bounds the rotation angle
body: If $\gamma\le p\le1/2$ then $\sin(2\theta)=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\ge\sqrt{\gamma}$.
If γ ≤ p ≤ 1/2 then sin(2θ) = 2√(p(1 − p)) ≥ √γ.

title: A random Grover iteration count gives success probability at least $9/20$
A random Grover iteration count gives success probability at least 9/20
body: If $\gamma\le p\le1/2$ and $M=\lceil10/\sqrt{\gamma}\rceil$, then $\frac1M\sum_{\ell=0}^{M-1}\sin^2((2\ell+1)\theta)\ge\frac12-\frac1{2M\lvert\sin(2\theta)\rvert}\ge\frac9{20}$.
If γ ≤ p ≤ 1/2 and M = ⌈10/√γ⌉, then (1/M) ∑ from ℓ = 0 to M − 1 of sin²((2ℓ + 1)θ) ≥ 1/2 − 1/(2M|sin(2θ)|) ≥ 9/20.

lem-3.1.title: Uniform bounded amplitude amplification
body: For $0<\gamma\le1/2$ and $0<\eta<1/2$ there is a single procedure, black-box in $A$ and $A^{-1}$ and with call counts depending only on $\gamma$ and $\eta$, using $O(\gamma^{-1/2}\log(1/\eta))$ calls for every $p$ and on every branch, such that for every state preparation $A$ with a success bit, success probability $p$ and, if $p>0$, normalized successful state $\lvert g\rangle$: it reports failure or produces a successful outcome; conditional on success the output is $\lvert g\rangle$ up to global phase; if $p\ge\gamma$, failure probability $\le\eta$; if $p=0$ it always reports failure.

For 0 < γ ≤ 1/2 and 0 < η < 1/2 there is a single procedure, black-box in A and A⁻¹ and with call counts depending only on γ and η, using O(γ⁻¹ᐟ² log(1/η)) calls for every p and on every branch, such that for every state preparation A with a success bit, success probability p and, if p > 0, normalized successful state |g⟩: it reports failure or produces a successful outcome; conditional on success the output is |g⟩ up to global phase; if p ≥ γ, failure probability ≤ η; if p = 0 it always reports failure.

def-aij.title: Measured probabilities of coherent comparisons
body: For a fixed oracle input and a coherent comparison circuit, $a_{ij}$ is the probability that $i$ is reported as defeating $j$ when the result is measured, using one circuit per unordered pair; $a_{ii}=0$.
For a fixed oracle input and a coherent comparison circuit, aᵢⱼ is the probability that i is reported as defeating j when the result is measured, using one circuit per unordered pair; aᵢᵢ = 0.

eq-10.title: Complementary comparisons with zero diagonal
body: $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=1$ for $i\ne j$, and $a_{ii}=0$.
aᵢⱼ + aⱼᵢ = 1 for i ≠ j, and aᵢᵢ = 0.

def-T-eps.title: Tournament length and comparison error budget
body: For $m\ge2$: $T=\lceil\log_2(1000m)\rceil$, $\varepsilon=1/(1000T)$.

eq-11.title: A dominant candidate beats every opponent
body: $i_*$ is dominant if $a_{i_*j}\ge1-\varepsilon$ for every $j\ne i_*$.
i★ is dominant if aᵢ★ⱼ ≥ 1 − ε for every j ≠ i★.

def-ideal-process.title: Weighted pivot sampling and elimination
body: Ideal process: $w_i=1$ for all $i$, $W=\sum_i w_i$. While $W>0$ sample $p$ with probability $w_p/W$, append $p$ to the list, update by equation (12). If $W=0$, leave list and weights unchanged. Run $T$ steps.
Ideal process: wᵢ = 1 for all i, W = ∑ᵢ wᵢ. While W > 0 sample p with probability wₚ/W, append p to the list, update by equation (12). If W = 0, leave list and weights unchanged. Run T steps.

eq-12.title: Multiply candidate weights by pivot comparisons
body: Update $w_i\leftarrow w_i a_{ip}$ for all $i\in[m]$.
Update wᵢ ← wᵢ aᵢₚ for all i ∈ [m].

title: One random pivot leaves at most $W/2$ in expectation
One random pivot leaves at most W/2 in expectation
body: For $W>0$: $\mathbb{E}[W_{\mathrm{new}}\mid w]=\frac1W\sum_{p,i}w_pw_i a_{ip}=\frac{W^2-\sum_i w_i^2}{2W}\le W/2$.
For W > 0: E[W_new | w] = (1/W) ∑ₚ,ᵢ wₚ wᵢ aᵢₚ = (W² − ∑ᵢ wᵢ²)/(2W) ≤ W/2.

title: After $T$ ideal pivots, expected weight is at most $m/2^T$
After T ideal pivots, expected weight is at most m/2ᵀ
body: The bound of equation (13) also holds when $W=0$, hence $\mathbb{E}[W_T]\le m/2^T$.
The bound of equation (13) also holds when W = 0, hence E[W_T] ≤ m/2ᵀ.

claim-weight-lb.title: A dominant candidate retains weight above one half until selected
body: If $i_*$ satisfies equation (11) and has not been selected in $t\le T$ steps, then $w_{i_*}\ge(1-\varepsilon)^t\ge1-T\varepsilon>1/2$. Hence $W>0$ until it is selected.
If i★ satisfies equation (11) and has not been selected in t ≤ T steps, then wᵢ★ ≥ (1 − ε)ᵗ ≥ 1 − Tε > 1/2. Hence W > 0 until it is selected.

eq-14.title: Markov bounds the chance of missing a dominant candidate
body: $\Pr[i_*\text{ absent from the ideal list}]\le\Pr[W_T\ge1/2]\le2m/2^T$.
Pr[i★ absent from the ideal list] ≤ Pr[W_T ≥ 1/2] ≤ 2m/2ᵀ.

construct-sampler.title: Amplify a coherent sample of surviving candidates
body: Given pivots $p_1,\ldots,p_t$ with $t<T$: prepare uniform $\lvert i\rangle$ over $[m]$, compare $i$ with each pivot in a fresh workspace, set the success bit if and only if every comparison says $i$ defeats its pivot, keeping all garbage. Apply Lemma 3.1 with $\gamma=1/(2m)$, $\eta=\varepsilon$. On failure stop and return the accumulated list; otherwise measure the index, append, and continue for at most $T$ stages.

Given pivots p₁, …, pₜ with t < T: prepare uniform |i⟩ over [m], compare i with each pivot in a fresh workspace, set the success bit if and only if every comparison says i defeats its pivot, keeping all garbage. Apply Lemma 3.1 with γ = 1/(2m), η = ε. On failure stop and return the accumulated list; otherwise measure the index, append, and continue for at most T stages.

eq-15.title: The coherent state before success measurement
body: Pre-success state: $m^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^m\lvert i\rangle\bigotimes_{b=1}^t\lvert\phi(i,p_b)\rangle$.
Pre-success state: m⁻¹ᐟ² ∑ from i = 1 to m of |i⟩ ⊗ from b = 1 to t of |φ(i, pᵦ)⟩.

claim-success-prob.title: Success conditioning realizes the exact weighted pivot law
body: Conditional on index $i$ the success probability is $\prod_{b=1}^t a_{ip_b}=w_i$ (empty product $1$). Total success probability is $W/m$, and conditional on success the index has law $w_i/W$ exactly.
Conditional on index i the success probability is ∏ from b = 1 to t of aᵢ,ₚᵦ = wᵢ (empty product 1). Total success probability is W/m, and conditional on success the index has law wᵢ/W exactly.

claim-coupling.title: Couple the quantum sampler to the ideal tournament
body: Until $i_*$ is first selected, $W/m\ge1/(2m)$, so at each such history the sampler fails with probability $\le\varepsilon$ and otherwise follows the exact ideal pivot law. The real list contains $i_*$ except with probability $\le2m/2^T+T\varepsilon$.

Until i★ is first selected, W/m ≥ 1/(2m), so at each such history the sampler fails with probability ≤ ε and otherwise follows the exact ideal pivot law. The real list contains i★ except with probability ≤ 2m/2ᵀ + Tε.

claim-tournament-cost.title: A fixed query cap for every tournament branch
body: Stage $t$ uses $O(c(t+1))$ queries per call; Lemma 3.1 uses $O(\sqrt m\log(1/\varepsilon))$ calls; the sum over $t<T$ is $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$, a fixed cap on every branch.
Stage t uses O(c(t + 1)) queries per call; Lemma 3.1 uses O(√m log(1/ε)) calls; the sum over t < T is O(c√m T² log T), a fixed cap on every branch.

prop-3.2.title: The quantum tournament lists a dominant candidate with high probability
body: Let $m\ge2$, $T=\lceil\log_2(1000m)\rceil$, $\varepsilon=1/(1000T)$. For a coherent comparison circuit controlled by two candidate indices, reversible with all workspace retained, using at most $c\ge1$ bit queries, with probabilities $a_{ij}$ satisfying equation (10), there is a quantum algorithm making $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries on every branch and returning a list of at most $T$ candidates such that, for every fixed oracle input and every $i_*$ satisfying equation (11), the list contains $i_*$ with probability $\ge1-2m/2^T-T\varepsilon$.

Let m ≥ 2, T = ⌈log₂(1000m)⌉, ε = 1/(1000T). For a coherent comparison circuit controlled by two candidate indices, reversible with all workspace retained, using at most c ≥ 1 bit queries, with probabilities aᵢⱼ satisfying equation (10), there is a quantum algorithm making O(c√m T² log T) queries on every branch and returning a list of at most T candidates such that, for every fixed oracle input and every i★ satisfying equation (11), the list contains i★ with probability ≥ 1 − 2m/2ᵀ − Tε.

def-decode.title: Decode an address with error reduction
body: $\operatorname{decode}(i)$: run the algorithm of Lemma 2.1(ii) on each $A_{i,h}$, $h\in[r]$, with error $\le\varepsilon/r$, retaining workspace. Output a string in $\{0,1\}^r$ on every input.
decode(i): run the algorithm of Lemma 2.1(ii) on each Aᵢ,ₕ, h ∈ [r], with error ≤ ε/r, retaining workspace. Output a string in the set of length-r binary strings on every input.

claim-decode-cost.title: Address decoding costs only polylogarithmically many queries
body: $\operatorname{decode}$ uses $O_k(r\log(r/\varepsilon))=(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$ queries. If all $r$ instances are defined, the address is correct with probability $\ge1-\varepsilon$. Otherwise it still returns some address.
decode uses Oₖ(r log(r/ε)) = (log m) to the power Oₖ(1) queries. If all r instances are defined, the address is correct with probability ≥ 1 − ε. Otherwise it still returns some address.

def-comparison.title: Compare two columns through their decoded pointers
def-comparison.body: For two distinct columns, first sort them and decode each in a separate workspace. At each decoded address, read the column’s pointer toward its opponent and inspect the selected bit of the opponent’s data string. A column disqualifies its opponent when that bit is zero. If exactly one column disqualifies the other, that column wins; otherwise, the smaller index wins. A self-comparison returns false without reading a pointer.

claim-comparison-state.title: Coherent comparison matches the classical probabilities
body: The comparison uses $c=(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$ queries, and reversing it costs the same. Its measurement probabilities agree with the classical description because later operations are controlled on the decoded registers in the computational basis. The resulting comparison probabilities $a_{ij}$ satisfy the pairwise comparison identities in equation (10).

The comparison uses c = (log m) raised to Oₖ(1) queries, and reversing it costs the same. Its measurement probabilities agree with the classical description because later operations are controlled on the decoded registers in the computational basis. The resulting comparison probabilities aᵢⱼ satisfy the pairwise comparison identities in equation (10).

claim-winner-dominates.title: A winner defeats every rival with high probability
body: If $i_*$ is a winning column, then for every $j\ne i_*$, its comparison probability satisfies $a_{i_*j}\ge1-\epsilon$. This holds on every input, whether or not the opponent’s partial-function instances are defined.
If i★ is a winning column, then for every j ≠ i★, its comparison probability satisfies aᵢ★ⱼ ≥ 1 − ε. This holds on every input, whether or not the opponent’s partial-function instances are defined.

def-verify.title: Verify a candidate by searching for a failed local test
body: To verify column $i$, decode and measure a fresh address $s$. Let $A$ prepare a uniform test index and the exact failing-test flag at $(i,s)$, with $K$ tests. Apply the amplification lemma with $\gamma=1/K$ and $\eta=\epsilon$. Reject if a failed test is found; otherwise accept. Output one exactly when some listed candidate is accepted.

To verify column i, decode and measure a fresh address s. Let A prepare a uniform test index and the exact failing-test flag at (i, s), with K tests. Apply the amplification lemma with γ = 1/K and η = ε. Reject if a failed test is found; otherwise accept. Output one exactly when some listed candidate is accepted.

claim-verify.title: Verification accepts winners and rejects nonwinners with bounded error
body: A nonwinning column is accepted with probability at most $\epsilon$ at every address. A true winner is rejected with probability at most $\epsilon$, solely because of a decoding error. The search costs $O(\sqrt K\log(1/\epsilon)\log m)=\sqrt m\,(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$ queries, plus the cost of decoding.

A nonwinning column is accepted with probability at most ε at every address. A true winner is rejected with probability at most ε, solely because of a decoding error. The search costs O(√K log(1/ε) log m) = √m (log m) raised to Oₖ(1) queries, plus the cost of decoding.

claim-error.title: The tournament and verification errors remain bounded
body: On a zero-input, the error probability is at most $T\epsilon$. On a one-input, it is at most $2m/2^T+T\epsilon+\epsilon<1/3$.
On a zero-input, the error probability is at most Tε. On a one-input, it is at most 2m/2ᵀ + Tε + ε < 1/3.

claim-coherent-access.title: Superposed array access uses ordinary bit queries
body: Every superposed array access is implemented with ordinary bit queries. Compute the global bit index reversibly. Reading a pointer uses $O(\log m)$ queries. A controlled query uses load, use and unload, for two queries in total.

Every superposed array access is implemented with ordinary bit queries. Compute the global bit index reversibly. Reading a pointer uses O(log m) queries. A controlled query uses load, use and unload, for two queries in total.

prop-3.3.title: The quantum query upper bound
body: For every fixed $k\ge2$, the total function satisfies $Q(F_{k,m})\le\sqrt m\,(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$.
For every fixed k ≥ 2, the total function satisfies Q(Fₖ,ₘ) ≤ √m (log m) raised to Oₖ(1).

claim-product-law.title: Conditioning on a transcript preserves a product law
body: For a deterministic algorithm and every transcript $\tau$ of positive probability, the conditional law of $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$ given $\tau$ is a product of separate conditional laws. This holds because the event of obtaining $\tau$ is a Cartesian product of constraints on the separate inputs.

For a deterministic algorithm and every transcript τ of positive probability, the conditional law of (U₁, …, Uᵣ) given τ is a product of separate conditional laws. This holds because the event of obtaining τ is a Cartesian product of constraints on the separate inputs.

def-value-V.title: The best success probability within the remaining budget
body: After $q_h$ queries to $U_h$, define $V_h(\tau)$ as the largest success probability for computing $P(U_h)$ under its conditional law given $\tau$, using at most $L-q_h$ further queries.
After qₕ queries to Uₕ, define Vₕ(τ) as the largest success probability for computing P(Uₕ) under its conditional law given τ, using at most L − qₕ further queries.

eq-16.title: One query cannot increase the expected remaining value
body: If the next query at transcript $\tau$ addresses input $U_h$, then $\mathbb E[V_h(\tau^{\prime})\mid\tau]\le V_h(\tau)$. The conditional laws and remaining budgets of all other inputs are unchanged.
If the next query at transcript τ addresses input Uₕ, then E[Vₕ(τ′) ∣ τ] ≤ Vₕ(τ). The conditional laws and remaining budgets of all other inputs are unchanged.

claim-supermartingale.title: The product of remaining values is a supermartingale
body: The remaining-value product satisfies $\mathbb E[\prod_j V_j(\tau^{\prime})\mid\tau]\le\prod_j V_j(\tau)$. It is a supermartingale over at most $rL$ queries.
The remaining-value product satisfies E[∏ⱼ Vⱼ(τ′) ∣ τ] ≤ ∏ⱼ Vⱼ(τ). It is a supermartingale over at most rL queries.

claim-final-bound.title: Final joint success is bounded by the value product
body: At the final transcript $\tau$, the chosen output vector satisfies $\Pr[\text{chosen vector correct}\mid\tau]\le\prod_h\max_b\Pr[P(U_h)=b\mid\tau]\le\prod_h V_h(\tau)$.
At the final transcript τ, the chosen output vector satisfies Pr[chosen vector correct ∣ τ] ≤ ∏ₕ maxᵦ Pr[P(Uₕ) = b ∣ τ] ≤ ∏ₕ Vₕ(τ).

lem-4.1.title: Separate query caps force a direct-product success bound
body: Let $P:D\to\{0,1\}$, where $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$. Let $\mu$ be a distribution on $D$ and let $L$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose every deterministic algorithm making at most $L$ queries computes $P$ under $\mu$ with success probability at most $\beta$. If $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ are independent with common law $\mu$, every classical algorithm making at most $L$ queries to each $U_h$ outputs $(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r))$ with probability at most $\beta^r$. The algorithm may be randomized, may adapt among the $r$ inputs, and may receive arbitrary additional information independent of $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$.

Let P: D → Boolean, where D is a subset of the length-n Boolean strings. Let μ be a distribution on D and let L be a nonnegative integer. Suppose every deterministic algorithm making at most L queries computes P under μ with success probability at most β. If U₁, …, Uᵣ are independent with common law μ, every classical algorithm making at most L queries to each Uₕ outputs (P(U₁), …, P(Uᵣ)) with probability at most βʳ. The algorithm may be randomized, may adapt among the r inputs, and may receive arbitrary additional information independent of (U₁, …, Uᵣ).

claim-minimax-mu.title: Minimax supplies one hard promised-input distribution
body: If $L<R(P)$, there is a distribution $\mu$ on the nonempty domain of $P$ such that every deterministic tree of depth at most $L$ has success probability at most $2/3$ under $\mu$.
If L < R(P), there is a distribution μ on the nonempty domain of P such that every deterministic tree of depth at most L has success probability at most 2/3 under μ.

eq-17.title: The query budget for the randomized lower bound
body: Set $G=\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$.
Set G = ⌊mL/100⌋.

def-dummy.title: The dummy input has one random zero in each column
body: Construct the dummy input $Y^{(0)}$ as follows. Independently for each column $i$, choose $J_i$ uniformly from $[m]$ and give $X_i$ a single zero at position $J_i$. All $A_{i,h}$ are independent with common law $\mu$, independently of all $J_i$. Fill every cell $B_{i,s}$ with one fixed blank pattern.

Construct the dummy input Y⁽⁰⁾ as follows. Independently for each column i, choose Jᵢ uniformly from [m] and give Xᵢ a single zero at position Jᵢ. All Aᵢ,ₕ are independent with common law μ, independently of all Jᵢ. Fill every cell Bᵢ,ₛ with one fixed blank pattern.

def-planted.title: Plant a winner at one independently chosen column
body: Choose $I$ uniformly from $[m]$, independently of $Y^{(0)}$. Obtain $Y^{(1)}$ from $Y^{(0)}$ by setting $X_I=1^m$ and filling $B_{I,s_I}$ with the correct transcripts and the pointers $p_{I,s_I,j}=J_j$ for every $j\ne I$.
Choose I uniformly from [m], independently of Y⁽⁰⁾. Obtain Y⁽¹⁾ from Y⁽⁰⁾ by setting X_I = 1ᵐ and filling B_(I,s_I) with the correct transcripts and the pointers p_(I,s_I,j) = Jⱼ for every j ≠ I.

claim-Y-values.title: The dummy input has value zero and the planted input has value one
body: For every sample point, $F_{k,m}(Y^{(0)})=0$ and $F_{k,m}(Y^{(1)})=1$.
For every sample point, Fₖ,ₘ(Y⁽⁰⁾) = 0 and Fₖ,ₘ(Y⁽¹⁾) = 1.

eq-18.title: Distinguishing the inputs requires querying a changed bit
body: For a deterministic algorithm making at most $G$ queries, $\left|\Pr[\text{outputs one on }Y^{(1)}]-\Pr[\text{outputs one on }Y^{(0)}]\right|\le\Pr[\text{dummy run queries }X_I[J_I]]+\Pr[\text{dummy run queries any bit of }B_{I,s_I}]$.
For a deterministic algorithm making at most G queries, |Pr[outputs one on Y⁽¹⁾] − Pr[outputs one on Y⁽⁰⁾]| ≤ Pr[dummy run queries X_I[J_I]] + Pr[dummy run queries any bit of B_(I,s_I)].

def-Z.title: Count the zeros discovered on the dummy run
body: Let $Z$ be the number of columns whose zero is discovered during the dummy run.
Let Z be the number of columns whose zero is discovered during the dummy run.

claim-uniform-zero.title: An undiscovered zero remains uniform over unqueried positions
claim-uniform-zero.body: Before a column’s zero is found, its position is uniform among that column’s unqueried positions, conditional on the full adaptive transcript.

claim-EZ.title: Early and late discoveries bound the expected zero count
body: The expected number of discovered zeros satisfies $\mathbb E Z\le4G/m$. An early discovery has fewer than $m/2$ distinct positions queried in its column before it; its probability is at most $2/m$ per query, contributing at most $2G/m$ in expectation. Every other discovery occurs in one of at most $2G/m$ columns receiving at least $m/2$ queries.

The expected number of discovered zeros satisfies E Z ≤ 4G/m. An early discovery has fewer than m/2 distinct positions queried in its column before it; its probability is at most 2/m per query, contributing at most 2G/m in expectation. Every other discovery occurs in one of at most 2G/m columns receiving at least m/2 queries.

eq-19.title: A random column’s zero is rarely queried
body: The probability that the dummy run queries the erased zero is $\Pr[\text{dummy run queries }X_I[J_I]]=\mathbb E Z/m\le4G/m^2$.
The probability that the dummy run queries the erased zero is Pr[dummy run queries X_I[J_I]] = E Z/m ≤ 4G/m².

def-heavy.title: A heavy column exceeds the total input-query threshold
body: Column $i$ is heavy if, over the entire dummy run, the algorithm makes more than $L$ queries in total to $A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}$. Repeated queries count.
Column i is heavy if, over the entire dummy run, the algorithm makes more than L queries in total to Aᵢ,₁, …, Aᵢ,ᵣ. Repeated queries count.

eq-20.title: A uniformly selected column is rarely heavy
body: The probability that the selected column is heavy satisfies $\Pr[I\text{ is heavy}]\le G/(mL)$.
The probability that the selected column is heavy satisfies Pr[I is heavy] ≤ G/(mL).

def-simulator.title: A capped simulation extracts an address from a proposed query
body: Fix a column $i$ and a query time $t\in\{1,\ldots,G\}$. A simulator receives the entire dummy input outside $A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}$ and runs the deterministic algorithm up to its proposed $t$-th query. It aborts before query number $L+1$ to those $r$ strings in total. If it reaches time $t$ and the proposed query is to a cell $B_{i,s}$, it outputs $s$; otherwise it outputs a fixed vector.

Fix a column i and a query time t from 1 to G. A simulator receives the entire dummy input outside Aᵢ,₁, …, Aᵢ,ᵣ and runs the deterministic algorithm up to its proposed t-th query. It aborts before query number L + 1 to those r strings in total. If it reaches time t and the proposed query is to a cell Bᵢ,ₛ, it outputs s; otherwise it outputs a fixed vector.

eq-21.title: At a fixed time, hitting the true cell while its column stays light is rare
body: For every column $i$ and query time $t$, $\Pr[i\text{ is nonheavy and the }t\text{-th query is in }B_{i,s_i}]\le(2/3)^r$.
For every column i and query time t, Pr[i is nonheavy and the t-th query is in B_(i,s_i)] ≤ (2/3)ʳ.

eq-22.title: Heavy columns and address guessing bound true-cell access
body: The probability of querying the planted true-address cell is $\Pr[\text{dummy run queries }B_{I,s_I}]\le G/(mL)+G(2/3)^r$.
The probability of querying the planted true-address cell is Pr[dummy run queries B_(I,s_I)] ≤ G/(mL) + G(2/3)ʳ.

eq-23.title: The three error terms bound distinguishing advantage
body: The absolute difference between the output-one probabilities on the planted and dummy inputs is at most $4G/m^2+G/(mL)+G(2/3)^r$.
The absolute difference between the output-one probabilities on the planted and dummy inputs is at most 4G/m² + G/(mL) + G(2/3)ʳ.

claim-tail.title: The address-guessing tail tends to zero
body: The tail term satisfies $G(2/3)^r\le\frac1{100}m^{2-20\log_2(3/2)}=o(1)$.
The tail term satisfies G(2/3)ʳ ≤ (1/100)m^(2 − 20 log₂(3/2)) = o(1).

claim-numeric.title: Elementary bounds on the total error
body: For $m=4^t$, $r=40t$, $1\le L\le m$ and $G\le mL/100$: $4G/m^2\le 4/100$, $G/(mL)\le 1/100$, and $G(2/3)^r\le 1/100$, so the bound in equation (23) is at most $6/100<1/3$.
For m = 4ᵗ, r = 40t, 1 ≤ L ≤ m and G ≤ mL/100: 4G/m² ≤ 4/100, G/(mL) ≤ 1/100, and G(2/3)ʳ ≤ 1/100, so the bound in equation (23) is at most 6/100 < 1/3.

prop-4.2.title: Randomized lower bound for the total construction
body: For each fixed integer $k\ge 2$ and every sufficiently large power of four $m$, $R(F_{k,m})>G=\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$, with $L=\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/(\log_2 m)^2\rfloor$.
For each fixed integer k ≥ 2 and every sufficiently large power of four m, R(Fₖ,ₘ) > G = ⌊mL/100⌋, with L = ⌊m^(1−1/k)/(log₂ m)²⌋.

cor-R-omega.title: Asymptotic randomized lower bound
body: For fixed $k$, $R(F_{k,m})=\Omega_k\!\left(m^{2-1/k}/(\log m)^2\right)$.
For fixed k, R(Fₖ,ₘ) = Ωₖ(m^(2−1/k)/(log m)²).

claim-floor.title: Floors preserve the asymptotic lower bound
body: For sufficiently large $m$, $\left\lfloor (m/100)\left\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/(\log m)^2\right\rfloor\right\rfloor\ge c_k m^{2-1/k}/(\log m)^2$ after decreasing $c_k>0$.
For sufficiently large m, ⌊(m/100)⌊m^(1−1/k)/(log m)²⌋⌋ ≥ cₖ m^(2−1/k)/(log m)² after decreasing cₖ > 0.

claim-exponent-ratio.title: Every smaller exponent gives an unbounded ratio
body: For fixed $0\le\alpha<4$ and integer $k\ge 2$ with $2-1/k>\alpha/2$: $\frac{R(F_{k,m})}{(1+Q(F_{k,m}))^\alpha}\ge\frac{c_{k,\alpha}m^{2-1/k-\alpha/2}}{(\log m)^{2+\alpha b_k}}$, which tends to infinity.
For fixed 0 ≤ α < 4 and integer k ≥ 2 with 2−1/k > α/2: R(Fₖ,ₘ)/(1+Q(Fₖ,ₘ))^α ≥ cₖ,α m^(2−1/k−α/2)/(log m)^(2+αbₖ), which tends to infinity.

claim-no-smaller-exponent.title: No exponent below four suffices
body: For every $0\le\alpha<4$, $\alpha$ does not belong to the set in equation (1), because a suitable $k$ exists with $k>1/(2-\alpha/2)$.
For every 0 ≤ α < 4, α does not belong to the set in equation (1), because a suitable k exists with k > 1/(2−α/2).

title: Deterministic query complexity $D(f)$
Deterministic query complexity D(f)
body: $D(f)$ is the least depth of a deterministic decision tree computing $f$ exactly on every input.
D(f) is the least depth of a deterministic decision tree computing f exactly on every input.

def-deg.title: Multilinear polynomial degree
body: $\deg(f)$ is the degree of the unique real multilinear polynomial agreeing with $f$ on the cube, with degree zero for every constant function, including the zero function. With this convention it is unchanged by replacing input or output bits by signs.

deg(f) is the degree of the unique real multilinear polynomial agreeing with f on the cube, with degree zero for every constant function, including the zero function. With this convention it is unchanged by replacing input or output bits by signs.

def-bs.title: Block sensitivity
body: A nonempty $B\subseteq[n]$ is a sensitive block at $x$ if flipping all bits of $B$ changes $f(x)$. $\operatorname{bs}(f)$ is the maximum over $x$ of the number of pairwise disjoint sensitive blocks at $x$.
A nonempty B ⊆ [n] is a sensitive block at x if flipping all bits of B changes f(x). bs(f) is the maximum over x of the number of pairwise disjoint sensitive blocks at x.

def-Gamma-i.title: Coordinate-filtered adversary matrices
body: For an input-indexed matrix $\Gamma$, $(\Gamma_i)_{xy}=\Gamma_{xy}\mathbf{1}\{x_i\ne y_i\}$. Matrix norms are operator norms for the Euclidean norm.
For an input-indexed matrix Γ, (Γᵢ)ₓᵧ = Γₓᵧ 1[xᵢ ≠ yᵢ]. Matrix norms are operator norms for the Euclidean norm.

claim-perron.title: A nonnegative leading eigenvector
body: A nonzero real symmetric entrywise nonnegative $\Gamma$ has a nonnegative unit eigenvector $v$ of eigenvalue $\lVert\Gamma\rVert$.
A nonzero real symmetric entrywise nonnegative Γ has a nonnegative unit eigenvector v of eigenvalue ‖Γ‖.

def-adv-progress.title: The adversary progress function
body: $W_t=\sum_{x,y}v_xv_y\Gamma_{xy}\langle\psi_x^t\mid\psi_y^t\rangle$, where $\psi_x^t$ is the purified state after $t$ queries on input $x$.
Wₜ = ∑ₓ,ᵧ vₓvᵧΓₓᵧ⟨ψₓᵗ | ψᵧᵗ⟩, where ψₓᵗ is the purified state after t queries on input x.

claim-per-query.title: Progress changes by a bounded amount per query
body: Each query changes $W$ by at most $|W_{t+1}-W_t|\le 2\sum_i u_i^{\mathsf T}\Gamma_i u_i\le 2\max_i\lVert\Gamma_i\rVert$, where $u_i(x)=v_x\lVert\phi_{x,i}\rVert$.
Each query changes W by at most |Wₜ₊₁−Wₜ| ≤ 2∑ᵢ uᵢᵀΓᵢuᵢ ≤ 2 maxᵢ ‖Γᵢ‖, where uᵢ(x) = vₓ‖φₓ,ᵢ‖.

claim-final-overlap.title: Successful outputs force a small final overlap
body: If $\Pr[\text{output }1]$ is $\le 1/3$ on one state and $\ge 2/3$ on another, their overlap has absolute value $\le 2\sqrt{2}/3$. Hence $|W_{\mathrm{final}}|\le (2\sqrt{2}/3)\lVert\Gamma\rVert$.
If Pr[output 1] is ≤ 1/3 on one state and ≥ 2/3 on another, their overlap has absolute value ≤ 2√2/3. Hence |W_final| ≤ (2√2/3)‖Γ‖.

lem-A.2.title: The nonnegative adversary lower bound
body: Let $f$ be a nonconstant total Boolean function, and $\Gamma$ a nonzero real symmetric entrywise nonnegative input-indexed matrix with $\Gamma_{xy}=0$ whenever $f(x)=f(y)$. Then $Q(f)\ge c\lVert\Gamma\rVert/\max_i\lVert\Gamma_i\rVert$ for an absolute constant $c>0$.

Let f be a nonconstant total Boolean function, and Γ a nonzero real symmetric entrywise nonnegative input-indexed matrix with Γₓᵧ = 0 whenever f(x)=f(y). Then Q(f) ≥ c‖Γ‖/maxᵢ ‖Γᵢ‖ for an absolute constant c > 0.

def-Sf.title: The sensitivity graph and its spectral norm
body: $S_f$ is the adjacency matrix on $\{0,1\}^n$ of the graph joining inputs that differ in exactly one bit and have different $f$-values. $\lambda(f)=\lVert S_f\rVert$.
S_f is the adjacency matrix on the Boolean n-cube of the graph joining inputs that differ in exactly one bit and have different f-values. λ(f) = ‖S_f‖.

lem-A.3.bs.title: Block sensitivity is quadratically bounded by quantum complexity
body: For nonconstant total $f$, $\operatorname{bs}(f)=O(Q(f)^2)$.
For nonconstant total f, bs(f) = O(Q(f)²).

lem-A.3.lambda.title: Sensitivity spectral norm is bounded by quantum complexity
body: For nonconstant total $f$, $\lambda(f)=O(Q(f))$.
For nonconstant total f, λ(f) = O(Q(f)).

lem-A.3.title: Quantum bounds for both sensitivity parameters
body: For nonconstant total $f$, both $\operatorname{bs}(f)=O(Q(f)^2)$ and $\lambda(f)=O(Q(f))$ hold, the conjunction of the two sensitivity bounds.
For nonconstant total f, both bs(f) = O(Q(f)²) and λ(f) = O(Q(f)) hold, the conjunction of the two sensitivity bounds.

claim-restrict-parity.title: A full-degree restriction agrees with parity on a majority
body: With $f$ in sign form and $d=\deg f\ge 1$, restricting variables outside a degree-$d$ monomial's support gives $g$ on the $d$-cube with nonzero parity correlation. So for some $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, $U=\{x:g(x)=\sigma x_1\cdots x_d\}$ has $|U|>2^{d-1}$, and every cube edge inside $U$ changes $g$.

With f in sign form and d = deg f ≥ 1, restricting variables outside a degree-d monomial's support gives g on the d-cube with nonzero parity correlation. So for some σ equal to −1 or 1, U = the set of x satisfying g(x) = σx₁⋯x_d has |U| > 2^(d−1), and every cube edge inside U changes g.

def-huang.title: The signed cube adjacency matrices
body: $H'_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $H'_{j+1}=\begin{pmatrix}H'_j&I\\I&-H'_j\end{pmatrix}$. Its entrywise absolute value is the cube adjacency matrix.
H′₁ = [[0,1],[1,0]], H′ⱼ₊₁ = [[H′ⱼ,I],[I,−H′ⱼ]]. Its entrywise absolute value is the cube adjacency matrix.

claim-huang-spectrum.title: The spectrum of the signed cube adjacency matrix
body: For $d\ge 1$, $(H'_d)^2=dI$ and $\operatorname{tr}H'_d=0$; $H'_d$ has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt d$, each of multiplicity $2^{d-1}$.
For d ≥ 1, (H′_d)² = dI and tr H′_d = 0; H′_d has eigenvalues ±√d, each of multiplicity 2^(d−1).

claim-interlace.title: A large induced cube subgraph has a large Rayleigh quotient
body: There is a nonzero $v$ in the $\sqrt d$-eigenspace supported on $U$; with $u=|v|$, $u^{\mathsf T}A_Uu\ge v^{\mathsf T}H'_dv=\sqrt d\lVert u\rVert^2$.
There is a nonzero v in the √d-eigenspace supported on U; with u=|v|, uᵀA_Uu ≥ vᵀH′_dv = √d‖u‖².

lem-A.4.title: Degree is at most the squared sensitivity spectral norm
body: Every nonconstant total Boolean $f$ satisfies $\deg(f)\le\lambda(f)^2$.
Every nonconstant total Boolean f satisfies deg(f) ≤ λ(f)².

claim-round-block.title: Each monomial-query round produces a disjoint sensitive block
body: In each round of the algorithm on input $x$, with $S$ the selected maximum-degree monomial's support in the current restriction, the restriction to $S$ with all other unqueried variables set as in $x$ is nonconstant. So some nonempty subset of $S$ is a sensitive block at $x$. Blocks of different rounds are disjoint.

In each round of the algorithm on input x, with S the selected maximum-degree monomial's support in the current restriction, the restriction to S with all other unqueried variables set as in x is nonconstant. So some nonempty subset of S is a sensitive block at x. Blocks of different rounds are disjoint.

lem-A.5.title: Deterministic complexity is bounded by block sensitivity times degree
body: Every total Boolean $f$ satisfies $D(f)\le\operatorname{bs}(f)\deg(f)$.
Every total Boolean f satisfies D(f) ≤ bs(f) deg(f).

thm-A.1.title: The universal quartic upper bound
body: Every total Boolean function satisfies $R(f)\le D(f)=O((1+Q(f))^4)$, with an absolute constant.
Every total Boolean function satisfies R(f) ≤ D(f) = O((1+Q(f))⁴), with an absolute constant.

claim-address-guess.title: Independent copies make the whole address hard to guess
body: Under $\mu$ from the minimax distribution claim, for $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ independent and identically distributed with law $\mu$, every classical algorithm making at most $L$ queries to each $U_h$, given information independent of $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$, outputs $(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r))$ with probability $\le(2/3)^r$.

Under μ from the minimax distribution claim, for U₁,…,Uᵣ independent and identically distributed with law μ, every classical algorithm making at most L queries to each U_h, given information independent of (U₁,…,Uᵣ), outputs (P(U₁),…,P(Uᵣ)) with probability ≤ (2/3)ʳ.

title: Hardness of $P$ gives a randomized lower bound for the total function
Hardness of P gives a randomized lower bound for the total function
body: Let $m=4^t$ with $t\ge 1$ and $r=40t$. Let $P$ be a partial function on $km$ bits with an exact circuit $C$ ($d=1$ if and only if defined, and $d=1$ implies $b=P$), and $F$ the total function built from $(P,C)$. If $1\le L\le m$ and $L<R(P)$, then $R(F)>\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$.

Let m = 4ᵗ with t ≥ 1 and r = 40t. Let P be a partial function on km bits with an exact circuit C (d=1 if and only if defined, and d=1 implies b=P), and F the total function built from (P,C). If 1 ≤ L ≤ m and L<R(P), then R(F) > ⌊mL/100⌋.

claim-winner-fidelity.title: The formal winner predicate matches the paper
body: By the circuit correctness guarantee in Lemma 2.1(iii), $\operatorname{WinsAt}(y,i,s)$ if and only if $X_i=1^m$, every $P(A_{i,h})$ is defined, $s=s_i$, the transcripts in $B_{i,s}$ are correct, and equation (8) holds. Hence $\exists s,\;\operatorname{WinsAt}(y,i,s)$ is the paper's winner condition.

By the circuit correctness guarantee in Lemma 2.1(iii), WinsAt(y,i,s) if and only if Xᵢ = 1ᵐ, every P(Aᵢ,ₕ) is defined, s = sᵢ, the transcripts in Bᵢ,ₛ are correct, and equation (8) holds. Hence there exists s such that WinsAt(y,i,s) is the paper's winner condition.
